speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singaporeans are naturally worried that this will lead to more people here, especially the vulnerable, falling severely ill.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, there are concerns that this will trigger a fresh infection wave that can bring back social restrictions and undo what we have painstakingly achieved over the past three years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government, and certainly, the Multi-Ministry Task Force (MTF) and the Ministry of Health (MOH), are acutely aware of these concerns because protecting Singaporeans and maintaining our freedom and normal lives have been our primary objectives throughout this pandemic journey.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As I have said a few times publicly over the past months, the pandemic is not over and we need to be especially mindful that when China opens up, there will be risks and uncertainties because the virus would be sweeping through a population of 1.4 billion, mostly COVID-19 naive, and that is now happening.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition, we have also anticipated that there would be a "winter wave" of infections across countries in the Northern hemisphere.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This has also happened in many countries, such as the US, Europe, Japan and South Korea.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Prior to this, many countries have dismantled all their border measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A few have now reinstated the measures and announced new measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As for Singapore, we have never dismantled all of our border measures and have kept relevant measures, precisely because we anticipated these risks.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, I will explain why we decided on our current measures and why they are appropriate, given our current context and circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But before that, let me report on the outcomes of the measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After all, the proof of the pudding is in the eating.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Cases had fallen, so sometimes, it can be 15% to 20%.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By and large, throughout the pandemic, 5% to 10% of the total cases reported every day.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The four weeks running up to 1 January 2023 was probably one of the most difficult periods of the epidemic in China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is a low number because every day, our total reported cases is about 1,000.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: ASEAN countries accounted for over 50%, rest of Asia around 15%, Europe – 11% and the Middle East – 9%.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Amongst all of our imported cases, in that four weeks, seven developed severe illnesses and had to be hospitalised.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Three were from the Middle East, two from ASEAN, one from Europe, one from China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most were Singaporeans returning from these countries and regions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And these were not large numbers, so the impact on our healthcare system was very small.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Since 1 January 2023 till today, I did a further check.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There have also been no severe infection cases coming from China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Why is it that travellers from China accounted for a very small percentage of imported infections and severe cases, when China is experiencing such a huge infection wave?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is due to the measures we put in place, and it is backed up by our high vaccination coverage which is being kept up-to-date.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, travel volumes between Singapore and China have been very low throughout the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This translates to between 700 to 1,000 arrivals from China every day, less than 10% of pre-COVID-19 volume.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: China's opening up to the world is great news and something we are looking forward to, so that we can restore our rich and substantive people-to-people links.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As China opens up, the Ministry of Transport (MOT) will carefully calibrate any adjustments from the current low travel volume, at least until the infection wave has clearly subsided in China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many scientists believe that the current infection wave in China has already started to subside, especially the major Chinese cities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will probably take a few more weeks for the trend to be very clear and we can then progressively restore pre-COVID-19 flight volumes between our two countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second reason is that we have been maintaining a test requirement for at-risk travellers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Travellers have to either be fully vaccinated based on World health Organization (WHO) vaccination definitions or produce a negative pre-departure test (PDT) result before heading to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why when Singaporeans are overseas now, when you go to the airport, you try to check-in with an airline, you have to produce your vaccination certificates at the point of check-in.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is so that the airlines know, and we know, whether you are required to produce a negative PDT result before you are allowed to board the plane.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over the past months, many Singaporeans have actually written to me and to MOH to feedback that this current rule causes a lot of inconvenience.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And they asked, can it be done away with at the check-in counter, where they have to – "kalang kabut" or scrambling – to show their vaccination certificate?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of them have to log into their HealthHub with their Singpass and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We had been explaining to them that it is important to maintain it, to manage the risks that we are currently facing, because unvaccinated and infected travellers coming from anywhere in the world are at risk of severe infection and can add to our healthcare workload.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Spain, one of the most highly vaccinated countries in Europe, has just announced that they are implementing the same test requirement as Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in summary, there are three groups of countries with varied responses as a result of China opening up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, most of ASEAN, the Middle East, Africa, South America, New Zealand – which are not imposing any border measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Thailand, we thought, is putting on some of these requirements; I just read that it is taking them off again.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we are neither the tightest nor the most liberal, but somewhere in-between.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we do not discriminate because these severe cases can originate from any country, any region in the world, as shown by our data.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I cannot speak for other countries, but I will now explain why the measures have worked so far for us and are appropriate in our current context.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Minister Iswaran will further elaborate on what MOT is doing with regard to air travel.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The measures may work now, but not permanently.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will continually assess the situation and, if need be, make adjustments or implement new measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At all times, our decisions must be based on science, on evidence and on data.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To do so, it is worthwhile recapitulating how far we have come.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the early stages of the pandemic, infections were our primary concern, because it was a disease that could lead to many severe episodes and deaths, and there were no vaccines or treatments available.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Under those circumstances, we adopted a zero-COVID-19 policy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That meant tight border measures, testing every passenger and quarantining them before allowing them to move around in our community.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The same considerations applied within the community, where we implemented contact tracing, quarantined close contacts, imposed strict safe management measures (SMMs), including a circuit breaker.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, effective vaccines were developed, and they changed our considerations fundamentally.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With the great majority of our population vaccinated and many recovered safely from relatively mild infections, our population has developed strong hybrid immunity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the probability of COVID-19 infections leading to severe illnesses or deaths for our population has become very low, comparable to influenza or pneumococcal infections, both of which are endemic diseases that we have been living with for many years and which we have also been encouraging vaccinations for.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Based on the severity rate today, annual deaths caused by COVID-19 infections is similar to that caused by influenza infections.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, with extensive vaccination coverage, we can treat COVID-19 as an endemic disease.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Like influenza, top line infection numbers should no longer be our pre-occupation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Despite the high top line number, we carried on living life normally.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, we were watching the situation very carefully in our hospitals because it is the bottom line of number of severe cases and deaths that matter.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As it turned out, hospitals were very, very busy, but they were not overwhelmed and we rode through that wave.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our greater concern goes beyond hospital workload and capacity, to the evolution of the epidemic itself.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the infection waves around the world are driven by variants known to us – XBB, BA.2, BA.2.75, BA.5, BA.5.2, BN.1, BF.7, BQ.1, XBB.1.5 now.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We know their characteristics and that existing vaccines continue to be effective in preventing severe illnesses of these variants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What worries us most now, is the emergence of a new, unknown and more dangerous variant of concern.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our main worry is that with the virus continuing to spread throughout the world, there is a higher chance that a new variant of concern may emerge from anywhere in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It may possess worrying characteristics, escape vaccine protection, be more infectious, more likely to lead to severe illnesses, which would be very bad news.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A nightmare variant can knock us almost back to square one.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must then be prepared to hunker down.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We may need to reinstate measures, such as strict border controls, quarantine for travellers, social restrictions, including limits on group sizes, until a new and effective vaccine is developed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in short, our key concerns are: first, the emergence of a new and more dangerous variant, and second, even in the absence of a new dangerous variant, to protect our healthcare system against having too many severe cases.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And these set the context of our border measures in response to the infection wave in China and the winter wave in many countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The most common measures that we have read in the papers in response to the opening up of China is COVID-19 tests on travellers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But they do not help detect new variants of concern.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The tests tell us if the travellers are infected with COVID-19, but it does not identify the variant.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: New variants can emerge from anywhere in the world, not just China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, to detect new variants, we need an effective global surveillance system where samples from infected persons all around the world are systemically collected, the viral genomes sequenced and then shared on the global platform.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is best done by countries for their own local cases, rather than relying solely on traveller surveillance because they can only provide a delayed snapshot.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The most commonly used global COVID-19 genome sequencing platform is run by a non-profit organisation and it is called the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The data is publicly accessible and protects the ownership rights of the source country.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, GISAID hosts all shared genome sequences of the four viral pathogens of global interest currently: namely, COVID-19, influenza, Mpox and Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore actively contributes to GISAID, which in turn works with many countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: GISAID has established a base in Singapore in collaboration with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And MOH and GISAID have developed a strong working relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, when a major COVID-19 infection wave broke out in China, GISAID collaborated with the various Centres for Disease Controls, or CDCs, in major Chinese cities and provinces to obtain viral sequencing data.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Just today, you can now find genome sequences also from the province of Anhui, just fresh; it came out today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The data is analysed and processed from their office in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our local sequencing efforts on infected travellers from China further support this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The majority, as I mentioned, are BA.5.2 and BF.7 strains, which have already been detected in Singapore and other countries for many months.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our assessment is also consistent with that of WHO's Technical Advisory Group on SARS-CoV-2 Virus Evolution (TAG-VE), which released its findings on 4 January 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What we fear and worry most – a new dangerous variant that evades vaccine protection coming out from China as the virus spreads throughout their population – has not materialised yet.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we will continue to stay vigilant and plug ourselves deeply into the global surveillance system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When China announced that it will start to allow leisure visits in an orderly way, many people around the world is imagining a surge in COVID-19 infections from an increase of tourists from China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singaporeans, too, are asking if we should implement some of the measures other countries have announced and are implementing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, let us examine the effectiveness of these measures in protecting our hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, some countries conduct polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests on travellers from China after arrival.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the shortcoming of any on-arrival test is that they are done too late, because the travellers are already within our borders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, PCR tests are sensitive and bound to yield a large number of positive cases from countries that are experiencing or have just experienced a big wave.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even recovered travellers will shed dead viral fragments for quite some time, for a few weeks, even though they are no longer infectious.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We, therefore, did not consider doing this, as it would merely confirm what we expect, or what we already know.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For waste-water tests, it is best done on residential premises like dormitories and housing estates, because viral fragments can only be detected from solid wastes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the sample capture from plane toilets for a relatively short duration flight from China to Singapore is likely to be very small and of limited use.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That can be useful because it will sieve out COVID-19 positive passengers, prevent them from boarding the plane, reduce number of imported infections and, hence, severe cases and the burden on our hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, as I explained earlier, there is already low travel volume between Singapore and China, which is currently only less than 10% of pre-COVID-19 norms.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This already limits the number of imported infections more so than imposing a blanket PDT requirement on all travellers from China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I believe China is also acting cautiously and increasing outbound traffic in steps, and not make a sudden full opening.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we impose PDT on all travellers from China, the question will also arise: how about travellers from other regions that contributed to more infections and severe cases?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How about local community settings which we know are conducive to spreading the disease and can drive infection numbers and severe cases?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, by triggering PDT on travellers from one part of the world experiencing high infection numbers, are we contributing to an international precedent of imposing tests on travellers from countries experiencing an infection wave?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How will other countries treat travellers from Singapore when we encounter another infection wave?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead of imposing a blanket PDT specifically on travellers from one region or one country, we decided very early on that we should encourage adequate vaccination amongst all travellers coming to Singapore, from all parts of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This directly reduces the risk of importing severe cases and protecting our hospital system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why we have, until now, maintained the requirement that incoming travellers either are fully vaccinated based on the WHO's definition, or have to undergo a professionally administered or supervised PDT.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In Mandarin):   China's opening up to the world is a major milestone in the world's fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is great news for many countries, industries, enterprises, families and individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To Singapore, this is also an important development because it allows us to restore our rich and substantive people-to-people links.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Although what we yearned for has indeed happened, many people are worried that this could trigger a fresh wave of infection in Singapore and bring back social restrictions, and the freedom we have worked so hard for the past several years might also be lost.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH is acutely aware of these concerns and will remain highly vigilant.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Therefore, we need to use science, evidence and data to formulate the most effective COVID-19 policies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last December was probably one of the most difficult periods of the pandemic in China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Currently, most COVID-19 positive cases are mild, especially for those who have been vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, what we need to focus on are those severe cases who need to be hospitalised.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most of them were Singaporeans returning from these countries and regions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are not large numbers, so the impact on our healthcare system was very limited.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Why is it that travellers from China account for such a small percentage of our imported infections and severe cases, despite China experiencing a big infection wave?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The main reason is because travel volumes between Singapore and China have been very low throughout the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This translates to between 700 to 1,000 arrivals from China every day, less than 10% from pre-COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition, we have been maintaining a test requirement for at-risk travellers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These travellers have to be either fully vaccinated or produce a negative PDT result before heading to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is precisely because we have anticipated the situation today that we have kept these two very important border measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many scientists believe that the current infection wave has already started to subside in China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: During this difficult period, these measures have proved to be effective to keep Singapore's COVID-19 situation stable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, it is impossible that measures can work permanently.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The MTF will continue to monitor the ever-changing situation and review our measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If needed, we will change our COVID-19 measures accordingly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, the emergence of a new and more dangerous variant, and second, to protect our healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A new variant of concern may emerge from any part of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To detect new variants as soon as possible, we need an effective global surveillance system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: GISAID now collaborates with the various CDCs in major Chinese cities and provinces to obtain viral sequencing data.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Sichuan, Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Fujian, Inner Mongolia and Anhui contribute up-to-date viral genome sequences to GISAID on a weekly basis.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The data is analysed and processed in their office in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The GISAID data so far shows that the pandemic in China is driven by variants that are well-known and have already been circulating in other parts of the world, and current vaccines are effective against these variants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To protect our healthcare system, it is most important to encourage all travellers coming to Singapore from any part of the world to have adequate vaccination.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This directly reduces the risk of importing severe cases, and hence, protects our own hospital system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ultimately, our best defence is also what everyone can do – to get vaccinated and make sure our vaccination is up to date.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some people ask me: "We keep going for one booster shot after another.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When will these vaccinations come to an end?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When can we stop vaccination for COVID-19?" To be honest, COVID-19 vaccination has become part of the new norm.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Just like any other endemic diseases like influenza, we encourage people to go for vaccinations every year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will help prevent many from falling severely ill or even death.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As Prime Minister Lee said in his New Year's Day message, if the situation continues to be stable after the year-end holiday season and the infection wave in China, we can look forward to making final adjustments to our remaining social restrictions to establish a post-pandemic normalcy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the latest worry about the outbreak in China is part of the new norm.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Tomorrow, another region may experience a major wave.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, many regions in the Northern Hemisphere are experiencing rising infections of both COVID-19 and influenza over the winter season.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: New infection waves are bound to start in Singapore from time to time, over and over again, as variants with immune escape emerge, protection from vaccines and previous infections wane, and re-infections increase.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While we step up global surveillance and consider border measures whenever we feel threatened, remember the best defence – and which every one of us can play a part –  is to have up-to-date vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some people are asking when the vaccination is going to end.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How many shots of booster must we take?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To be very honest, COVID-19 vaccinations have become part of the new norm.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For an endemic disease like influenza, vaccinations are encouraged every year, which will help avoid many deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The current situation, where we feel threatened by rising infections around us, is a clear illustration why vaccination needs to be an integral part of our ongoing defence against an endemic COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am heartened that most Singaporeans are responding to this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As we move into this new norm, we will never be complacent, but our responses need to be based on science, evidence and data.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are ready to adjust policies whenever necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will always do our best to maintain our way of life and not go back to the days of lockdowns, unless absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister S Iswaran will be making a related Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will allow Members to raise points of clarifications on both Statements after this Statement.
